'''''Dahlia imperialis''''', or '''bell tree dahlia''', is a large [[flowering plant]] of the family [[Asteraceae]], native to the Americas.

== Description ==
Growing between {{Convert|8–10|m|abbr=off}} tall, it is a herbaceous [[perennial]], rapidly growing in springtime from its [[tuber]], after a dormant winter period (which may be brief in mild climates). From its underground base, the plant will begin sending up hollow, cane-like, 4-sided stems with swollen nodes and large, [[tripinnate]] leaves; foliage near the ground is quickly shed. 

The pendant or nodding flowerheads are {{Convert|7.5–15|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} across, with [[ray floret]]s, typically a lavender or mauvish-pink in colour.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Dayle E. Saar, Neil O. Polans & Paul D. Sørensen |year=2003 |title=A phylogenetic analysis of the genus ''Dahlia'' (Asteraceae) based on internal and external transcribed spacer regions of nuclear ribosomal DNA |journal=[[Systematic Botany]] |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=627–639 |jstor=25063902 |doi=10.1043/01-78.1|doi-broken-date=11 July 2025 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0889-1575(92)90005-5 |title=Nutrient content of selected indigenous leafy vegetables consumed by the Kekchi people of Alta Verapaz, Guatemala |journal=Journal of Food Composition and Analysis |volume=5 |pages=25–34 |year=1992 |last1=Booth |first1=Sarah |last2=Bressani |first2=Ricardo |last3=Johns |first3=Timothy }}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
After some ''Dahlia'' species were brought from [[Mexico]] to Europe in the 16th century, ''D. imperialis'' was first described in 1863 by [[Benedikt Roezl]] (1823–1885), the great [[Czechs|Czech]] orchid collector and traveller who, ten years later (in 1872–73), embarked on a plant odyssey through the Americas.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.ipni.org/ | title=The International Plant Names Index – home page}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is native to Mexico, [[Belize]], [[Guatemala]], [[Honduras]], [[El Salvador]], [[Nicaragua]], [[Costa Rica]], [[Panama]] and south into [[Colombia]] and [[Ecuador]]. It is a plant of the [[Highland (geography)|uplands]], mainly found in the foothills of subtropical or tropical mountains (above the humidity of the lower forests), at elevations around {{convert|1500|-|1700|m|abbr=on}}.

==Cultivation==
This species is fast-growing, the [[growth spurt]] being linked to shorter daylight hours; the tree dahlia usually comes into flower in autumn, before the risk of frost. [[Plant propagation|Propagation]] is by seed or by [[Cutting (plant)|stem cuttings]], around {{convert|30|cm|abbr=on}} long and having at least two [[Node (plants)|nodes]], laid horizontally about 5–10 cm under the soil; top-dressing with pea [[gravel]], decomposed [[granite]], or [[Grit (supplement)|grit]] is optional but helpful for moisture retention, erosion control and additional drainage.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.strangewonderfulthings.com/105.htm | title=Dahlia imperialis – Tree Dahlia}}</ref>

=== Uses ===
Many tuberous dahlia can be prepared and consumed like potatoes or cooked carrots. Additionally, the petals can be eaten on green salads or soups, and tree dahlia leaves are used as a dietary supplement by the [[Q'eqchi' people]] of [[San Pedro Carchá]], [[Alta Verapaz]], [[Guatemala]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=S. Booth, T. Johns & C. Y. Lopez-Palacios |year=1993 |title=Factors influencing the dietary intake of indigenous leafy greens by the K'ekchi people of Alta Verapaz, Guatemala |journal=Ecology of Food and Nutrition |volume=31 |issue=1 & 2 |pages=127–145 |doi=10.1080/03670244.1993.9991354|bibcode=1993EcoFN..31..127B }}</ref>
